title: Djöhandrai
dek: Djo hides, stammers and loves a good meal—and keeps choosing to help people in danger.
imageAlt: Portrait of Djöhandrai, also called Djo

facts.Seen with: A spectral feline figure called Sister
facts.Recurring choices: Tending wounds and staying close to companions
facts.Affiliation: Not a member of the Seekers

body:
Djöhandrai, usually called Djo, is a frightened feline adventurer who keeps finding reasons to help. He stammers, hides, runs from horrors and makes time for food. He also tends the wounded and follows companions into danger. His courage is visible because the fear stays visible too.

The person missing beside him

At the Gate, Djo asks where his sister is and whether he can go back. Being told there is no way home brings a mournful cry for her. Anáil offers a possibility: she can ask someone named Ada to send his sister through, though she cannot bring her immediately. This is Anáil’s offered hope, rather than a confirmed promise of reunion.

In a hurried personal note, Djo says he has made friends and hopes his sister would be proud, but he needs her beside him. His unfinished reference to “Moma and Popa” is followed by angry tears. The note connects his present loneliness to an earlier absence; it does not tell us exactly what happened to his parents.

“I’m alone again. Like when Moma and Popa—” — Djo’s scratched note

Scene sources: 1, 2, 3, 4.

Scene sources: 1.

“I was hiding first!”

Djo’s fear is something other people can see and share. When Timale jumps behind him, Djo objects: H-Hey, I was hiding first! Timale answers that Djo has nine lives and he only has one. The exchange is a joke between frightened companions, not proof of a literal ability to survive nine deaths.

Later, Djo finds a green hag beside an amalgamation of rotten bodies and immediately flees. These moments preserve his instinct to find cover without deciding everything he will do afterward.

Scene sources: 1, 2, 3, 4.

The wounded come first

In the July fight, Aurélia offers to make Djo faster. He is too focused on patching up an injured orc to answer immediately. His attention goes to the person bleeding beside him before his own combat advantage.

During the September harpy expedition, he admits he knows a little about treating cuts. When Di’trillio falls, he panics and nevertheless works to stem the bleeding with precision. He continues helping while Sister fights. His uncertainty about himself and the care he actually provides coexist in the same scenes.

Scene sources: 1, 2, 3, 4.

Sister, present but unexplained

At the September gathering, Djo introduces a cheerful, ghostly feline figure as Sister. She appears beside him in combat. When Natalia asks about the apparition, Djo calls it a long story and says he will explain later.

The visible companion and the name he gives her are established. Whether she is his original sister, how this manifestation came about, and whether Ada had any part in it remain unresolved here. These scenes do not identify Ada beyond Anáil’s acquaintance or show him causing Sister’s appearance.

Scene sources: 1, 2, 3.

“Don’t stray too far!”

In the later Old Earth Hills cave investigation, Djo wants to leave but chooses to help prevent the corpse’s fate from reaching others. He participates alongside the cave company; his presence does not make him a member of the Seekers.

When Saoirse moves on, Djo calls, W-Wait, Saoirse! Don’t stray too far! and follows as protective detail. She calls him brave and offers a cheese sandwich. He devours it while trying to thank her through cheesy bites. Warmth and comedy remain part of his bravery.

Scene sources: Cave choice, Helping, 1, 2, 3.

Sauce stains and uncomfortable questions

Djo arrives late to the September expedition after one more bowl of pasta. His food jokes give danger an ordinary scale, but they do not exhaust his character. A sauce-stained note about the Ahau shows him considering what people’s words might imply.

He describes them as pleasant but territorial, records their sensitivity about Cala and their hostility to devils, and worries that language about destructive fire suggests cleansing. These are Djo’s impressions and suspicions. The note does not establish an Ahau plan or settle Cala’s intentions.

Scene sources: 1.

Scene sources: 1.

Courage while afraid

Interpretation: the recurring movement in Djo’s story is from needing someone nearby to trying to stay nearby for others. Fear does not disappear; tending wounds, following companions and accepting their warmth give him ways to act through it. Reading this as a response to separation is supported by his own note, but remains a reading of the pattern rather than a stated explanation of every choice.

His significance stays personal: Sister’s place beside him, Timale’s shared fear, Aurélia’s offer during a fight, and Saoirse’s praise after danger. He becomes dependable without becoming invulnerable or losing the awkward voice and appetite that make him recognizable.

What remains open

  • What happened to Moma and Popa, and the circumstances of his separation from his sister.
  • Sister’s exact identity and manifestation, and any connection to Anáil’s hope about Ada.
  • Where his concerns about the Ahau lead, and how future losses may affect his protectiveness.

Source dates identify Discord posts, not an established in-world calendar. Djo’s Player Perspectives notes preserve his own understanding; the scene accounts show what he and his companions actually do.

profile.personality: Djo is visibly anxious, sincere and food-motivated. He hides, stammers and runs from frightening things, but repeatedly helps people while still afraid. His personal note connects present loneliness with an earlier absence involving Moma and Popa, whose circumstances remain unknown.
profile.achievements: Tends an injured orc before answering Aurélia’s offer of speed; treats fallen companions during the harpy expedition while Sister fights; joins the later cave investigation and follows Saoirse as protective detail. He is not a member of the Seekers.
profile.relationships: He arrived asking for his sister; Anáil offered to ask Ada for help. Later he introduces a spectral feline companion as Sister, whose exact identity remains unresolved. Timale shares his comic fear, Aurélia offers help in battle, and Saoirse praises his courage and gives him a sandwich.
